lessons.title: Tenses and subject–verb concord
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — grammar: tenses and concord (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Choose the right tense from the time markers in a sentence.
Make the verb agree with its real subject.
Handle tricky cases: neither…nor, collective nouns, ‘one of the…’, ‘each’, ‘as well as’.

blocks.title: The main tenses at a glance
blocks.md:
- **Present simple** (habits, facts): She **walks** to school.
- **Present continuous** (happening now): She **is walking** now.
- **Present perfect** (past linked to now): She **has walked** ten kilometres so far.
- **Past simple** (finished time): She **walked** home yesterday.
- **Past continuous** (in progress in the past): She **was walking** when it started to rain.
- **Past perfect** (the earlier past): She **had walked** home before the rain started.
- **Future**: She **will walk** tomorrow.

blocks.caption: The past perfect is further back than the past simple; the present perfect connects the past to now.
blocks.alt: A horizontal timeline. From left to right: a purple dot for the past perfect (had eaten), a blue dot for the past simple (ate), a green arc for the present perfect joining the past to a red line marked NOW, and an orange dot for the future (will eat).

blocks.title: Time markers
blocks.md:
- *yesterday, last week, two days ago, in 2020* → **past simple**
- *since, for, already, yet, just, ever, never, so far* → **present perfect**
- *by the time, before, after* + a past action → **past perfect** for the earlier action
- *now, at the moment, Look!* → **present continuous**
- *every day, usually, always, often* → **present simple**

Never use the present perfect with a finished time: ‘I have seen him yesterday’ is wrong; say ‘I saw him yesterday’.

blocks.title: Subject–verb concord: the rule
blocks.md:
A **singular** subject takes a **singular** verb; a **plural** subject takes a **plural** verb. In the present simple, a third-person singular subject adds **-s**: *The girl sings. The girls sing.*

Find the **real subject** and ignore the words in between: *The price of these shoes **is** high* (the subject is ‘price’, not ‘shoes’).

blocks.title: Tricky cases (1): joined subjects
blocks.md:
- **Neither… nor / either… or**: the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject. *Neither the teacher nor the students **were** late. Neither the students nor the teacher **was** late.*
- **As well as, together with, along with** do not change the subject. *The principal, as well as the teachers, **is** here.*
- **Each, every, everyone, everybody, nobody, either, neither** (used alone) are singular. *Each of the boys **has** a book.*

blocks.title: Tricky cases (2): groups and amounts
blocks.md:
- **Collective nouns** (family, team, committee, class, government): in British English, singular when the group acts as **one unit** (*The committee **has** made its decision*), plural when the **members act separately** (*The family **are** arguing among themselves*). Keep the verb and pronoun consistent.
- **One of the + plural noun** takes a singular verb: *One of the boys **is** absent.*
- **A number of** + plural → plural verb; **the number of** → singular verb.
- An amount seen as one sum is singular: *Five thousand francs **is** too much.*

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Find the verb, then ask ‘Who or what…?’ to find its **real subject**.
2. Decide: singular or plural? Apply the tricky-case rules if needed.
3. Look for a **time marker** (yesterday, since, by the time…) to choose the tense.
4. Check the form of irregular verbs (ring – rang – rung).
5. Read the sentence again: verb, pronouns and possessives must all agree.

blocks.title: Example 1: neither… nor + past simple
blocks.statement:
Put the verbs in brackets in the correct form:

‘Neither the prefect nor the students ___ (be) in class when the bell ___ (ring) yesterday.’

steps.md: The two subjects are joined by **neither… nor**: the verb agrees with the nearer one, ‘the students’, which is plural.
‘Yesterday’ is a finished time, so we need the **past simple**. Plural past simple of ‘be’: **were**.
‘Ring’ is irregular: ring – **rang** – rung. The past simple is ‘rang’ (not ‘rung’, which is the past participle).

blocks.answer: **Neither the prefect nor the students were in class when the bell rang yesterday.**

blocks.title: Example 2: ‘one of’ and ‘since’
blocks.statement:
Put the verbs in brackets in the correct form:

‘One of my brothers ___ (live) in Bamenda. He ___ (live) there since 2019, and my parents ___ (visit) him every Christmas.’

steps.md: The subject of the first verb is ‘One’ (not ‘brothers’): singular, present simple → **lives**.
‘Since 2019’ links a past starting point to now → **present perfect**: he **has lived** there since 2019.
‘Every Christmas’ is a habit → present simple. ‘My parents’ is plural → **visit** (no -s).

blocks.answer: **One of my brothers lives in Bamenda. He has lived there since 2019, and my parents visit him every Christmas.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Agreeing with the nearest noun: ‘The list of names are on the board’ ✗ → ‘The list of names **is** on the board’ ✓
- ‘One of the students have lost his bag’ ✗ → ‘One of the students **has** lost his bag’ ✓
- A finished time with the present perfect: ‘I have met her last year’ ✗ → ‘I **met** her last year’ ✓
- ‘Everyone are ready’ ✗ → ‘Everyone **is** ready’ ✓
- Singular nouns ending in -s: mathematics **is**, the news **is**, physics **is**.
- Inconsistency: ‘The team has lost their match’ ✗ → ‘The team has lost **its** match’ ✓

items: British and American English differ on collective nouns: British English often uses a plural verb (‘The team are playing well’), while American English prefers the singular. Both singular and plural can be correct in British English if you stay consistent.
Learn the irregular verbs in threes (go – went – gone, write – wrote – written): the past simple and the past participle are often confused.

reviewNotes: Collective nouns: the pack follows the usual British rule (singular for the group as a unit, plural for members acting separately). A teacher should confirm how strictly GCE markers apply it.

lessons.title: Reported speech
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — grammar: direct and reported speech (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Change statements from direct to reported speech (tenses, pronouns, time and place words).
Report yes/no questions and wh- questions with the correct word order.
Report commands and requests with ‘told / asked + object + to-infinitive’.

blocks.title: Direct and reported speech
blocks.md:
**Direct speech** gives the speaker's exact words between quotation marks: *Abena said, ‘I am tired.’*

**Reported (indirect) speech** gives the meaning without quotation marks: *Abena said that she was tired.*

When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told, asked), we usually change the **tense** one step back (backshift), the **pronouns** and the **time and place** words.

blocks.caption: Backshift: each tense moves one step into the past.
blocks.alt: Two columns of boxes joined by arrows. Direct speech on the left, reported speech on the right: present simple becomes past simple, present continuous becomes past continuous, present perfect becomes past perfect, past simple becomes past perfect, and will, can, may become would, could, might.

blocks.title: Pronouns, time and place
blocks.md:
- Pronouns follow the speaker: I → he / she; my → his / her; we → they; you → I / he / she / they (as the meaning requires).
- now → then; today → that day; tonight → that night
- yesterday → the day before / the previous day
- tomorrow → the next day / the following day
- last week → the week before; next week → the following week
- ago → before; here → there; this → that; these → those
- must → had to

blocks.title: Reporting questions
blocks.md:
- **Yes/no questions**: asked (+ object) + **if / whether** + statement word order. *‘Do you like rice?’ → He asked me **if I liked** rice.*
- **Wh- questions**: asked + **wh- word** + statement word order. *‘Where do you live?’ → She asked me **where I lived**.*

In reported questions: no question mark, no ‘do / does / did’, and the subject comes **before** the verb.

blocks.title: Reporting commands and requests
blocks.md:
Use **told / ordered / asked / advised + object + (not) to + infinitive**.
- *‘Close the door.’ → He told me **to close** the door.*
- *‘Don't shout!’ → She told us **not to shout**.*
- *‘Please help me.’ → He asked me **to help** him.*

Remember: **say** has no person object (*said that…*, *said to me*); **tell** needs one (*told me that…*).

blocks.title: When the tense does not change
blocks.md:
- The reporting verb is in the present: *He says, ‘I am tired.’ → He says that he **is** tired.*
- A general truth may keep the present: *The teacher said that water **boils** at 100 °C.*
- A situation that is still true may keep its tense, but at GCE level backshift is the safe choice unless a question says otherwise.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Choose the reporting verb: *said (that)*, *told + person*, *asked*.
2. Remove the quotation marks; add *that*, *if / whether*, a *wh-* word or *(not) to + infinitive*.
3. Change the pronouns and possessives to fit the speaker.
4. Move each tense one step back.
5. Change the time and place words.
6. Check the word order and the final full stop (no question mark).

blocks.title: Example 1: a statement
blocks.statement:
Put into reported speech:

Enanga said, ‘I am visiting my grandmother today, and I will come back tomorrow.’

steps.md: Reporting verb: *said* (no person object) + *that*. Pronouns: I → **she**, my → **her** (Enanga is a woman).
Time words: *today* → **that day**; *tomorrow* → **the next day**. We repeat ‘that’ after ‘and’ to keep the sentence clear.

blocks.answer: **Enanga said that she was visiting her grandmother that day and that she would come back the next day.**

blocks.title: Example 2: a question and a command
blocks.statement:
Put into reported speech:

The teacher said to Tanyi, ‘Why did you come late? Don't do it again.’

steps.md: The question: *asked Tanyi* + wh- word *why* + statement order. ‘Did you come’ loses *did* and moves back: **why he had come late**. No question mark.
The command: *told him* + **not to** + infinitive: **not to do it again**.
We join the two parts with *and*, using two different reporting verbs (asked… told…).

blocks.answer: **The teacher asked Tanyi why he had come late and told him not to do it again.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Question order: ‘She asked me where did I live’ ✗ → ‘She asked me **where I lived**’ ✓
- Keeping the question mark after a reported question.
- ‘He said me that…’ ✗ → ‘He **told me** that…’ or ‘He **said to me** that…’ ✓
- ‘She told him to don't shout’ ✗ → ‘She told him **not to shout**’ ✓
- Forgetting to change the pronouns or the time words (‘yesterday’ → ‘the day before’).
- ‘He asked that if…’ ✗ → ‘He asked **if**…’ ✓

items: Vary your reporting verbs in compositions: explained, complained, promised, warned, suggested, admitted, begged. Each one says something about the speaker's attitude.
‘Suggested’ follows its own pattern: ‘Let's go,’ he said → He suggested going / He suggested that we should go.

reviewNotes: Optional backshift (situations still true at the time of reporting): the advice ‘backshift is the safe choice at GCE level’ should be confirmed by a teacher.

exercises.prompt:
Choose the correct verb:

‘Neither my sister nor my cousins ___ coming to the party.’
exercises.explanation: With neither… nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: ‘my cousins’ is plural, so ‘are’.
exercises.method: Find the subject closest to the verb.
mistakes: Choosing ‘is’ because of ‘my sister’: she is further from the verb.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt:
Choose the correct verb:

‘We ___ in Douala since 2018.’
exercises.explanation: ‘Since 2018’ links a starting point in the past to now: this is the present perfect, ‘have lived’ (or ‘have been living’).
exercises.method: Since / for + a situation that continues up to now → present perfect.
mistakes: ‘We live here since 2018’ is a common error, often copied from French (‘nous habitons ici depuis 2018’).
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: True or false: the sentence ‘One of the students have lost his bag.’ is correct.
exercises.explanation: False. The subject is ‘One’, which is singular: ‘One of the students **has** lost his bag.’
exercises.method: Ask ‘Who has lost the bag?’ — one person, not all the students.
mistakes: Agreeing the verb with ‘students’, the noun just before it.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Match each time marker with the tense it usually calls for.
exercises.explanation:
- ‘since 2015’: from the past up to now → present perfect.
- ‘at the moment’: happening now → present continuous.
- ‘last Tuesday’: finished time → past simple.
- ‘by the time we arrived’: the action happened before another past action → past perfect.
- ‘every morning’: a habit → present simple.
exercises.method: Ask: finished time? up to now? before another past event? habit? now?
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt:
The paragraph below contains **five** errors of tense or concord. Rewrite it correctly.

‘Every morning, my brother and I walks to school. Yesterday, the teacher have gave us a test. The number of pupils who passed were small. Each of us have to do corrections, and neither the pupils nor the teacher were happy.’
exercises.model: Every morning, my brother and I **walk** to school. Yesterday, the teacher **gave** us a test. The number of pupils who passed **was** small. Each of us **has** to do corrections, and neither the pupils nor the teacher **was** happy.
rubric: 1 mark: walks → walk (plural subject ‘my brother and I’).
1 mark: have gave → gave (‘yesterday’ = past simple).
1 mark: were → was (‘the number of’ is singular).
1 mark: were → was (neither… nor: the nearer subject ‘the teacher’ is singular).
Deduct half a mark for any new error introduced.
exercises.explanation: Each error breaks one rule of the lesson: a compound subject (A and B) is plural; ‘yesterday’ rules out the present perfect; ‘the number of’ and ‘each’ are singular; with neither… nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
exercises.method: Take each verb one by one, find its real subject and its time marker.
mistakes: Changing ‘have gave’ to ‘have given’: the form is correct but ‘yesterday’ still requires the past simple.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct option to complete each sentence (1 mark each).
exercises.method: For each sentence: real subject, singular or plural, then time marker.
mistakes: Being misled by a noun ending in -s (Mathematics) or by a phrase between the subject and the verb.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.explanation: The committee acts as one unit, and the pronoun ‘its’ is singular, so the verb must be singular: ‘has’.
‘Mathematics’ ends in -s but is the name of one subject: it takes a singular verb.

parts.prompt: ‘By the time the doctor arrived, the patient ___.’
parts.explanation: The patient left before the doctor arrived (a past action): the earlier action takes the past perfect, ‘had left’.

parts.prompt: ‘The principal, together with the teachers, ___ the visitors every year.’
parts.explanation: ‘Together with the teachers’ does not change the subject, ‘the principal’ (singular). ‘Every year’ is a habit: present simple, ‘welcomes’.

parts.prompt: ‘Ten thousand francs ___ too much for a pair of sandals.’
parts.explanation: A sum of money seen as one amount takes a singular verb.

exercises.prompt:
‘Where are you going?’ she asked me.

Choose the correct reported form.
choices: She asked me where I was going.
She asked me where was I going.
She asked me where am I going?
She asked me where I am going?
exercises.explanation: A reported wh- question keeps the wh- word, uses statement order (subject before verb: ‘I was’), moves the tense back (are going → was going) and ends with a full stop.
exercises.method: wh- word + subject + verb, one tense back, no question mark.
mistakes: Keeping the question word order ‘was I going’.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt:
He said, ‘I saw the film yesterday.’

Choose the correct reported form.
choices: He said that he had seen the film the day before.
He said that he saw the film tomorrow.
He said that I had seen the film yesterday.
He said that he has seen the film the day before.
exercises.explanation: Three changes: I → he; past simple ‘saw’ → past perfect ‘had seen’; ‘yesterday’ → ‘the day before’.
exercises.method: Pronoun, tense, time word: check all three.
mistakes: Forgetting the pronoun change (‘that I had seen’).
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: True or false: the sentence ‘She told to me that she was tired.’ is correct.
exercises.explanation: False. ‘Tell’ takes a person object directly, without ‘to’: ‘She **told me** that she was tired.’ With ‘say’ we write ‘She said to me that…’ or ‘She said that…’.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Match each word from direct speech with the word usually used in reported speech (after a past reporting verb).
exercises.explanation: When we report later, the original ‘today’ is no longer today: time and place words shift to fit the moment of reporting. ‘The following day’ and ‘the previous day’ are also correct for ‘tomorrow’ and ‘yesterday’.
exercises.method: Imagine you are telling the story a week later: which words would still make sense?
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt:
Rewrite each sentence in reported speech.

(a) ‘I can't find my keys,’ said Mr Tabe.
(b) ‘Have you finished your homework?’ my mother asked me.
(c) ‘Don't play near the road,’ the policeman told the children.
exercises.model:
(a) Mr Tabe said that he could not find his keys.
(b) My mother asked me if (whether) I had finished my homework.
(c) The policeman told the children not to play near the road.
rubric: (a) 1 mark: he + could not / couldn't + his keys (all three changes needed).
(b) 1 mark: if / whether + I had finished + my homework, statement order, no question mark.
(c) 1 mark: told the children + not to play.
Half a mark only if one change is missing.
exercises.explanation: (a) is a statement: pronoun and possessive change, ‘can’ → ‘could’. (b) is a yes/no question: ‘if/whether’, statement order, present perfect → past perfect. (c) is a negative command: ‘told + object + not to + infinitive’.
exercises.method: Identify the type first: statement, question or command.
mistakes: (b) ‘asked me had I finished’: question order.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Direct and reported speech. Answer all the questions.
exercises.method: Statement, question or command? Then pronouns, tenses, time words, word order.
mistakes: Adding a question mark to a reported question.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.prompt: Rewrite in reported speech: ‘We will visit Kribi next week,’ the students said.
parts.model: The students said (that) they would visit Kribi the following week.
rubric: 1 mark: next week → the following week (or ‘the next week’).
parts.explanation: Pronoun: we → they. Tense: will → would. Time: next week → the following week.

parts.prompt: The nurse said to the patient, ‘Take this medicine twice a day.’ Choose the correct reported form.
choices: The nurse told the patient to take that medicine twice a day.
The nurse told the patient that take this medicine twice a day.
The nurse said the patient to take that medicine twice a day.
The nurse told the patient took that medicine twice a day.
parts.explanation: A command: told + object + to + infinitive. ‘This’ becomes ‘that’. ‘Said the patient to…’ is wrong: ‘say’ cannot take a person object without ‘to’.

parts.prompt: ‘Is the shop open?’ the woman asked. Choose the correct reported form.
choices: The woman asked if the shop was open.
The woman asked if was the shop open.
The woman asked is the shop open.
The woman asked that the shop is open?
parts.explanation: A yes/no question: if (or whether) + statement order (the shop was) + backshift (is → was), no question mark.

parts.prompt: Rewrite in direct speech: Musa asked me whether I had eaten.
rubric: 1 mark: a correct question in quotation marks with ‘you’ and a question mark. Accept ‘Did you eat?’ as well as ‘Have you eaten?’.
parts.explanation: Going back to direct speech reverses the changes: I → you, the past perfect goes forward (had eaten → have eaten or ate), question order and a question mark return.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct option to complete or rewrite each sentence (1 mark each).
exercises.method: Concord: find the real subject. Tense: find the time marker. Reported speech: pronouns, backshift, word order.
mistakes: Agreeing with the wrong subject after neither… nor.
Keeping question order in a reported question.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.prompt: ‘Neither the headmaster nor his deputies ___ present at the meeting yesterday.’
parts.explanation: Neither… nor: the verb agrees with the nearer subject, ‘his deputies’ (plural); ‘yesterday’ requires the past simple: ‘were’.
‘Since 2010’: a situation that started in the past and continues now → present perfect, ‘has worked’.

parts.prompt: ‘Where do you live?’ the officer asked me. Choose the correct reported form.
choices: The officer asked me where I lived.
The officer asked me where did I live.
The officer asked me where do I live?
The officer asked me that where I lived.
parts.explanation: Wh- word + statement order, no ‘do/did’, present → past, no question mark and no ‘that’ before the wh- word.

parts.prompt: ‘Don't touch the wires,’ the electrician said to us. Choose the correct reported form.
choices: The electrician told us not to touch the wires.
The electrician told us to don't touch the wires.
The electrician said us not touching the wires.
The electrician told to us that don't touch the wires.
parts.explanation: A negative command: told + object + not to + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: ‘Either the boys or their father ___ the car every Sunday.’
exercises.explanation: Either… or: the verb agrees with the nearer subject, ‘their father’ (singular); ‘every Sunday’ is a habit → ‘washes’.

exercises.prompt: Which time marker goes with the present perfect?
exercises.explanation: ‘Since’ links the past to now. The other markers refer to a finished time and require the past simple.

exercises.prompt: ‘Everyone in the class ___ ready.’
exercises.explanation: ‘Everyone’ is singular, so the verb is singular: ‘is’.

exercises.prompt: The past perfect (had + past participle) is used for:
choices: an action completed before another past action
exercises.explanation: The past perfect places an action further back in the past than another past action: ‘The bus had left when we arrived.’

exercises.prompt: ‘A number of pupils ___ absent today.’
exercises.explanation: ‘A number of’ means ‘several’: the subject is plural, so ‘are’. (But ‘The number of pupils is…’.)

exercises.prompt: In reported speech after ‘said’, ‘will’ usually becomes:
exercises.explanation: Backshift: will → would, can → could, may → might.

exercises.prompt: In reported speech, ‘tomorrow’ usually becomes:
exercises.explanation: ‘Tomorrow’ → ‘the next day’ or ‘the following day’.

exercises.prompt: Which reported question is correct?
choices: She asked me what my name was.
She asked me what was my name.
She asked me what is my name?
She asked me what my name was?
exercises.explanation: Statement order (my name was) and a full stop, not a question mark.

exercises.prompt: ‘Please sit down,’ he said to us. Which is the correct reported form?
choices: He asked us to sit down.
He said us to sit down.
He told to us sitting down.
exercises.explanation: A request: asked + object + to + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: When is backshift NOT necessary?
choices: When the reporting verb is in the present tense
When the sentence is a question
When the sentence contains a pronoun
When the speaker is a teacher
exercises.explanation: ‘He says he is tired’: with a present reporting verb, the tense does not change.
